strengths: Timely and clearly motivated problem: it is the first systematic PTQ study for large-scale 3D reconstruction transformers (VGGT), a model class whose deployment cost is a real bottleneck and whose compression has been unexplored.

Identifies model-specific failure modes (heavy-tailed activations from data-independent camera/register tokens; unstable calibration sets due to multi-view data complexity) that are plausibly distinct from 2D ViT/LLM settings, supported by empirical distribution analyses (Figs. 3, 7).

Strong empirical results: W4A4 retains ~98% of FP performance on camera pose (Co3Dv2) and point map estimation (DTU) with clear margins over well-adapted baselines (BRECQ, QDrop, GPTQ, SmoothQuant, QuaRot, DopQ-ViT), plus cross-dataset generalization (calibration only on Co3Dv2, evaluated on DTU).

Comprehensive evaluation: two tasks and datasets, multiple bit-widths (W8A8, W6A6, W4A4), ablations of each component (rotation/scale ordering, granularity, sampling strategy with variance over seeds), and real-hardware latency and memory measurements rather than only theoretical FLOP counts.

Reasonable theoretical grounding: an entropy-maximization argument (Theorem 3.2) motivates the cluster-then-sample calibration strategy, and the 'mu-coherent' argument motivates token-wise granularity; hyperparameters, calibration cost, and hardware details are documented, with a code release promise.

Practicality is well demonstrated: low calibration overhead (~2.7 GPU-hours on an RTX4090, +0.02GB), negligible latency overhead from DSFQ, and efficiency results consistent with the claimed 2.5x speedup / 3.7x memory reduction.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core technique is a combination of known ingredients — Hadamard rotation (QuaRot/QuIP), channel-wise smoothing (SmoothQuant), and fine-grained quantization — adapted to VGGT; the main new technical pieces (post-local smoothing applied after rotation, frame-correlation-based clustering) are relatively small design modifications.

Narrow scope of validation: experiments use only VGGT-1B; the 5B variant and other 3D foundation models (DUSt3R, MASt3R) are not tested, making it hard to judge whether the proposed fixes generalize beyond one architecture, despite the 'first framework for 3D reconstruction transformers' claim.

Theoretical contributions are thin: Theorem 3.2 is a standard maximum-entropy result whose assumptions (known sub-domain volumes, independence) are not realistic and whose connection to the actual heuristic (K-Means with K=8, percentile filtering) is loose; Lemma 3.1 is cited rather than established.

Evaluation lacks some standard considerations: no comparison against QAT or mixed-precision alternatives, no results on depth/dense-task metrics or downstream tracking, and the reported 'even improved metrics vs. FP under W8A8 on DTU' is not explained or analyzed.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'state-of-the-art across different benchmarks' rests on only two benchmarks; there is no analysis of failure cases at W4A4 (e.g., AUC@3 drop from 54.9 to 43.6), and sensitivity to K, the filtering percentile, and calibration set size is only partially explored.

The special-token problem is addressed only implicitly through rotation/smoothing; a simpler explicit treatment (e.g., quantizing or excluding special-token channels separately) is not compared against, leaving uncertainty about whether the full dual-smoothing machinery is necessary.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant problem: VGGT-style billion-scale 3D reconstruction transformers are expensive to deploy, and this appears to be the first systematic PTQ treatment of this model family.

Solid empirical results: clear improvements over reasonable baselines (RTN, BRECQ, QDrop, GPTQ, SmoothQuant, QuaRot, DopQ-ViT) at W8A8/W6A6/W4A4 on Co3Dv2 and DTU, including a cross-dataset generalization test (calibration on Co3Dv2, evaluation on DTU).

Good engineering hygiene: hardware latency measurements on real hardware (2.5x speedup, 3.7x memory reduction), calibration cost analysis, and ablations covering both the quantization architecture (Table 3, 5, 6) and the calibration sampling strategy (Fig. 5, 8) with multiple random seeds and variance reporting.
The observation about data-independent camera/register tokens inducing heavy-tailed activations is a genuinely useful model-specific insight that motivates the design.
Reproducibility statement is reasonable, with hyperparameters and settings described in the appendix and promised code release.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the proposed DSFQ is essentially a combination of well-established techniques — Hadamard rotation (QuaRot, SpinQuant-era ideas), channel-wise scaling (SmoothQuant), and fine-grained/token-wise quantization (Chee et al., Tseng et al.). The contribution is adapting known machinery to a new model rather than a new quantization principle, which weakens the case for a top-tier venue.

The theory is shallow: Lemma 3.1 is a standard CLT argument borrowed from prior work, and Theorem 3.2 is a trivial entropy-maximization result (uniform sampling maximizes entropy) proved with a textbook Lagrange multiplier derivation; it provides little actionable insight beyond 'cluster and sample uniformly', and the assumptions (known partitions, proportional volumes) are exactly what is unknown in practice.

The Noise-Filtered Diverse Sampling component is heuristic: the noise-score, thresholding percentile, K=8 clusters, and frame-correlation features are all design choices without justification or sensitivity analysis. Fig. 8's own admission that prior-knowledge-based clusterings give only slight improvements suggests the component's benefit is modest and possibly fragile.

Narrow evaluation scope: experiments are confined to a single model variant (VGGT-1B) and essentially two benchmarks (camera pose on Co3Dv2, point maps on DTU). No evaluation on the VGGT-2B variant, no point tracking or depth metrics, no other 3D reconstruction models (e.g., Dust3R/MASt3R) to support the claim of generality to 'billion-scale 3D transformers'.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'state-of-the-art results across different benchmarks' rests on two datasets; the claim of improved metrics over FP under W8A8 (Table 2) is likely noise from the calibration procedure but is presented as a strength without investigation.

Presentation issues undermine polish: citation errors (e.g., 'Krishnamoorthi, 1806'), inconsistent naming (Quarot vs. QuaRot), a garbled baseline attribution ('PTQ (Feng et al., 2025c)'), and typos ('Quantvggt', 'recontruction') suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

Missing comparisons to potentially relevant recent PTQ approaches for vision/3D models, and no discussion of how the method would handle other data-independent token designs, limiting the claimed broader applicability.

strengths: First systematic study of post-training quantization for VGGT / large-scale 3D reconstruction transformers — a timely and practically relevant problem, since these billion-parameter models are hard to deploy.

Clear identification of two model-specific challenges (data-independent special tokens inducing heavy-tailed activations, and unstable multi-view calibration sampling), with motivating visualizations (Fig. 3, Fig. 4).

The proposed DSFQ (global Hadamard rotation + post-local channel smoothing + fine-grained granularity) is well motivated, the order-of-operations analysis (Rot.-Scale vs. Scale-Rot. in Tab. 6) is a nice touch, and scale factors are fused into neighboring layers so there is no runtime overhead.

Comprehensive experiments: W8A8/W6A6/W4A4 across camera pose estimation (Co3Dv2) and point map estimation (DTU), against a broad set of strong PTQ baselines (BRECQ, QDrop, GPTQ, SmoothQuant, QuaRot, DopQ-ViT), with consistent and significant gains (e.g., 86.9 vs. 81.6 AUC@30 at W4A4).

Ablations cover each component (architecture, granularity, sampling strategy), variance over five random seeds is reported for calibration sampling, and practical costs (calibration time/memory, real-hardware latency and memory reduction: 3.65× memory, 2.49× speedup) are measured, supporting the efficiency claims.
Good reproducibility posture: hyperparameters, calibration details, theorem proof, and code release承诺 are provided.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core techniques are largely assembled from prior work — Hadamard rotation (QuaRot, QuIP), channel smoothing (SmoothQuant-style scaling), fine-grained quantization, and K-Means-based diverse calibration sampling. The main novelty is their adaptation to VGGT-specific issues rather than fundamentally new quantization machinery.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only VGGT-1B is quantized; no other 3D foundation models (e.g., DUSt3R, MASt3R, Fast3R) are tested, so it is unclear whether the analysis of special-token-induced outliers and the framework generalize beyond VGGT. The 'first PTQ framework for VGGT' framing somewhat overstates the significance of a single-model study.

Theorem 3.2 is essentially a standard entropy-maximization (uniform sampling) result with heavy notation; its assumptions (known sub-regions V_k, independence) are not satisfied in practice, so its connection to the actual NFDS algorithm is loose and its contribution is marginal.

Some experimental details are thin: the selection of the 400-sample candidate pool and threshold T=0.2, K=8 lack sensitivity analysis; only two benchmarks (Co3Dv2, DTU) are used; point map 'improvement over FP' at W8A8 (1.782 vs. 1.185 Acc.) suggests evaluation noise or distribution mismatch that deserves discussion.

Writing/presentation issues: several typos and citation errors (e.g., 'Krishnamoorthi, 1806'), some claims (e.g., 'maintaining 98%') rely on cherry-picked metrics, and parts of the method description (Eq. 6 scale computation) require careful reading to verify correctness.
Cross-domain generalization is tested only via Co3Dv2→DTU; more diverse out-of-distribution scenes (e.g., in-the-wild video) would strengthen the practical deployment claim.

strengths: First systematic PTQ study for billion-scale 3D reconstruction transformers (VGGT), an important and previously unexplored deployment problem; the identified VGGT-specific challenges (data-independent camera/register tokens causing heavy-tailed activations, multi-view calibration instability) are well-motivated with visualizations.

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: multiple tasks (camera pose on CO3Dv2, point map on DTU, point cloud reconstruction on 7-Scenes/NRGBD), multiple bit-widths (W8A8/W4A4), many strong baselines (GPTQ, SmoothQuant, QuaRot, AWQ, RepQ-ViT, DopQ-ViT, BRECQ, QDrop), and substantial W4A4 gains (e.g., 86.9 vs 81.8 AUC@30 over QuaRot).

Real-hardware efficiency analysis with CUTLASS on RTX 4090 (2.5× speedup, 3.7× compression), plus granular ablations on quantization granularity, sampling strategies (with seed variance), Hadamard/α sensitivity, calibration cost, and sequence-length scaling — supporting the practical claims.
Generality is addressed beyond the main model: results on Fast3R, mixed-precision/asymmetric/QAT variants, and comparison with an orthogonal acceleration method (FastVGGT).
Reproducibility seems good: hyperparameters, calibration protocol, and code release are described; supplementary materials include reconstruction files.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core technique is largely a composition of existing tools (QuaRot-style Hadamard rotation, SmoothQuant-style channel scaling, fine-grained quantization), with the main new contribution being the ordering (rotation-then-scale) and the VGGT-specific calibration sampling; the significance of the ordering choice is asserted but not deeply analyzed theoretically.

Theorem 3.2 is weakly specified and borderline trivial: key quantities ('scale' of a domain, X* = E(X) as an 'expectation input') are ill-defined, the proof assumes a uniform partition structure not justified in practice, and its practical impact on the final method (K-means on a 1-D frame-correlation vector) is a heuristic leap rather than a consequence of the theorem.

Ablation presentation has confusing/inconsistent notation (e.g., 'Rot.-Scale' vs 'DSFQ' description on page 10, '86.9×' AUC values in Table 9, 'Calibiration' typo), and the abstract/intro claim of 'surpassing SOTA with a great margin' is weaker at W8A8 where differences are marginal.

Generalization is demonstrated only within feed-forward 3D reconstruction transformers (VGGT, Fast3R); the extent to which DSFQ/NFDS would help other 3D models or even LLM/vision settings is unclear, limiting the scope of the claims.

Some baselines may be under-tuned for this architecture (e.g., SmoothQuant collapsing at W4A4), raising a mild concern about fairness of comparison; also the W4A4 evaluation protocol differences between Table 1 (full set) and Table 5 (first 200 sequences per class, FP 90.5 vs 89.5) make cross-table comparisons slightly inconsistent.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: post-training quantization of billion-scale 3D reconstruction transformers (VGGT), which has been largely unexplored.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple tasks (camera pose, point map, point cloud reconstruction), datasets (CO3Dv2, DTU, 7-Scenes, NRGBD), bit-widths (W8A8, W4A4), and many baseline methods, with large margins over prior PTQ methods at W4A4 (e.g., 86.9 vs. 81.8 AUC@30 vs. QuaRot).

Real-hardware deployment evidence (RTX 4090 with CUTLASS kernels), reporting actual latency (2.5x) and memory (3.7x) gains rather than only FLOPs, plus an ablation showing the proposed smoothing adds only ~0.2% latency.

Thorough ablation studies covering each component, quantization granularity, calibration hyperparameters, calibration cost, random seeds, and a comparison to a token-compression acceleration method (FastVGGT) and a second architecture (Fast3R).
Clear motivation grounded in model-specific analysis: data-independent camera/register tokens producing heavy-tailed activations, and instability of calibration sampling for multi-view data.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core components are direct adaptations of established techniques — random Hadamard rotation from QuaRot/QuIP#, channel smoothing from SmoothQuant, block-wise calibration from BRECQ/QDrop, and fine-grained token-wise quantization. The main contribution is a domain-specific combination rather than a new quantization principle; the gap over QuaRot at W4A4, while real, comes largely from applying known smoothing tools to a new model family.

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 3.2) is essentially a maximum-entropy argument that samples should be drawn proportionally to region prevalence; it is near-trivial and its connection to the practical heuristic (K-Means on a 1-D frame-similarity vector with uniform sampling) is loose, undermining the 'principle' framing.

Evaluation is heavily concentrated on a single model (VGGT-1B). The single Fast3R experiment in the appendix is the only cross-architecture evidence, and several key tasks (e.g., depth metrics on standard VGGT benchmarks, downstream 3D tasks like point tracking) are not evaluated. Generality of the identified 'special token' failure mode to other 3D foundation models remains weakly supported.

Some W4A4 gains are confounded: QuantVGGT uses dynamic token-wise activation quantization and a calibration pipeline with learnable parameters (closer to lightweight QAT), while several baselines may be evaluated with simpler configurations; a unified-protocol comparison would strengthen claims.

Writing and presentation issues reduce polish: typos ('Calibiration'), a confusing ablation section where method labels appear inconsistent (the text compares against '(DSFQ)' when describing the alternative, likely a mislabeled variant), malformed table entries with erroneous '×' symbols on accuracy metrics (Table 9), and red formatting artifacts (e.g., '+3.3' annotations).

Calibration dataset construction requires a 400-sample candidate pool from the target-domain training set and downstream-specific statistics; the method's dependence on in-domain calibration data and its behavior in true cross-domain settings (calibration on one dataset, deployment on very different scenes) are only lightly probed.

The 'first PTQ framework for VGGT' claim is narrow in scope; concurrent work on efficient VGGT variants exists (e.g., FastVGGT cited by the authors), and the contribution may be seen as an application paper for a specific model rather than a generalizable method, limiting impact beyond this sub-niche.

strengths: First systematic study of post-training quantization for VGGT-class billion-scale 3D reconstruction transformers, an important and previously unexplored deployment problem; the two identified failure modes (data-independent special tokens causing heavy-tailed activations, and unstable multi-view calibration sampling) are clearly motivated and empirically supported (Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 7).

Very large empirical gains at W4A4 across multiple tasks and datasets: e.g., AUC@30 of 86.9 vs. 81.8 for the strongest baseline (QuaRot) on CO3Dv2, with near-lossless results on DTU, 7-Scenes, and NRGBD, and generalization to Fast3R (Table 6), which supports claims of robustness beyond a single model.

Comprehensive and honest evaluation: extensive ablations of each component (Tables 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13), multi-seed variance analysis of calibration strategies (Fig. 5, Fig. 8), real-hardware latency and memory measurements with CUTLASS on an RTX 4090 (Tables 14, 15), calibration cost analysis, and a comparison against a non-quantization accelerator (FastVGGT, Table 7).

Practical relevance: 3.7x memory reduction and 2.5x measured speedup with ~98% accuracy retention, running on consumer GPUs with a fast (2.67 h) PTQ pipeline; code release promised and raw reconstruction files provided.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core DSFQ recipe is a combination of well-established techniques (random Hadamard rotation from QuaRot/QuIP#, channel-wise smoothing from SmoothQuant, fine-grained/token-wise granularity from prior PTQ work). The main contribution is adapting and ordering these components for VGGT rather than a fundamentally new quantization principle.

The theoretical content is weak. Lemma 3.1 (Gaussianity after Hadamard rotation) is cited rather than established for this setting, and Theorem 3.2 reduces to a standard maximum-entropy argument (uniform p_j = 1/N*) under idealized assumptions; its connection to the practical K-Means/frame-aware clustering is heuristic and not rigorously justified (the gap between 'proportional sampling by region scale' and 'uniform sampling within K clusters' is hand-waved as 'under mild assumptions').

Boundary cases of the claims: experiments cover only W8A8 and W4A4; no results at W2 or weight-only settings that would test the framework's limits. Improvement margins at W8A8 and W6A6 over QuaRot are small (within ~0.1-0.4), so the headline advantage is essentially confined to W4A4.

Evaluation scope is somewhat narrow: calibration data is drawn from CO3Dv2 while DTU/7-Scenes/NRGBD serve as out-of-domain tests, which is good, but all quantitative main results use VGGT-1B; camera pose evaluation is limited to CO3Dv2, and other standard 3D benchmarks (e.g., RealEstate10K) are absent.

Some presentation issues: inconsistent notation and labeling in the ablation text (page 10 text appears to swap 'Rot.-Scale' and 'DSFQ' relative to Table 4), minor typos ('Calibiration', 'Diversed', 'AUC@3+' arrows), and the claimed '3.7x compression' in the abstract vs. 3.65x in tables is slightly inconsistent.
